paragraphs.text: A [rougui](yancha:rougui) from the [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is), the range along the border of northern Fujian and Jiangxi. Rougui is a cultivar of these mountains that dates from the Qing dynasty. This leaf was finished with a heavy [charcoal roast](yancha:making), given in several rounds with weeks or months of rest between them. The roast dries the tea so it keeps, and a [full roast](yancha:roast-levels) keeps the longest. The heavier the roast, the longer a fresh tea is rested before it is drunk.

[Rock tea](yancha:definition) grows among the cliffs, in crevices and on ledges, in thin soil weathered from the rock, with heavy rain and fog through the year. The trade sorts this ground into [true rock, half rock and river bank](wuyi-mountains:zones), by how rocky it is and how near it lies to the scenic core. This tea carries the mountain's name without naming a zone, so the label alone does not say how close to the core the leaf grew.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.
